plans.title: Not responding and not breathing normally

steps.text: Keep doing chest compressions. Use the lock-in hold first, and the hold from behind if your pushes are not good enough.
Keep doing chest compressions. The holds above were studied for weightlessness, and which method to use in partial gravity: to be set by clinical review.
If you are trained, give rescue breaths after every 30 pushes, with a face shield or pocket mask if the kit lists one. If not, keep pushing without stopping.
If the kit lists a crew medical restraint system, strap the person to it first, then compress in the handstand, standard or straddling position. Without it, keep using the hold above.
If the kit lists an AED, attach the pads and do what its voice says. Shock only with the person restrained on a surface that does not carry electricity.
A crewmate who is not pushing writes down when they collapsed or were last seen well, what happened (an electric shock, smoke or toxic air, an injury, choking or a fall), and what the AED said last.
A crewmate who is not pushing watches for normal breathing, movement or waking up.

Only once they breathe normally again: clip the oximeter on a finger, hand warm and still, until it shows one steady number. Never pause compressions to do this. Never delay or stop chest compressions for this.
If they stop responding or stop breathing normally again, open Someone needs help again.
If the kit lists an airway device, venous access and medicines, use them as in the onboard procedure. Without them, keep up compressions.
Decide when to stop CPR, as the most medically qualified crewmember.
Only once they breathe normally again: decide when to take their blood pressure, with the cuff on the bare upper arm as the device instructions say.

items.text: Time of the collapse or when they were last seen well, what was seen, what the AED said last, and any change since.

steps.text: Keep checking their breathing the whole time.
Keep the airway open: head tilted back gently, chin lifted.
If a head or neck injury is possible, keep the head and neck in line with the body while you keep the airway open.

Only if they are breathing normally, roll them onto their side in the recovery position. If they are not breathing normally, go back to the first screen and start chest compressions. Whether the recovery position works as on Earth in partial gravity: to be set by clinical review.
In weightlessness, how to hold or strap them: to be set by clinical review.
Stay with them. Do not leave them alone.

Ask what happened just before: a blow to the head, a faint, a fit or an alarm. Ask how long they have been like this, whether they have diabetes or any known illness, whether they are on any treatment, and whether there is any injury or bleeding.

Clip the oximeter on a finger, hand warm, relaxed and still, until it shows one steady number. A normal number does not cancel serious symptoms. The level that needs action: to be set by clinical review. Never delay or stop keeping the airway open and watching their breathing for this.

Put the cuff on the bare upper arm and follow the device instructions, arm supported and still. The level that needs action: to be set by clinical review. Never delay or stop keeping the airway open and watching their breathing for this.
Take their temperature with the kit thermometer as its instructions say. Record the number and the time. Never delay or stop keeping the airway open and watching their breathing for this.

If they are already still in front of the cameras, read their breathing rate there. Never delay a step for it. If it fails, count their breaths and enter the number. Never delay or stop keeping the airway open and watching their breathing for this.
If their breathing stops or turns to gasping, go back to the first screen and start chest compressions at once.
If anything else changes, open Someone needs help again.
Oxygen if the kit lists an oxygen supply, and further care, as in the onboard procedure.

plans.title: Eye injury or something in the eye

steps.text: Do not rub the eye.
If an object is stuck in the eye, do not remove it and put no pressure on the eye. Any cover must rest on the bone around the eye, not on the eye.
Chemical, dust or grit in the eye: keep the eye open and keep rinsing with plenty of clean water for at least 20 minutes.
In weightlessness, water and dust float. Keep rinsing and soak up the floating water as you go.
Ask what got in or hit the eye, whether it was a chemical, dust or a sharp object, whether they can see as well as before, whether light hurts or it feels gritty, and whether contact lenses are in.
A crewmate repeats the sight check and the photo, and keeps both for the log.
Pain or a gritty feeling that does not settle after rinsing: tell the medical officer. How long to give it: to be set by clinical review.

Only once the rinse is done. Cover the other eye. Read the same text on the screen with each eye and record any difference. Test card and distance: to be set by clinical review. Never delay or stop rinsing for this.
Only once the rinse is done. Take a still, close photo of the eye in good light, kept for the medical officer and the log. Do not touch the eye. Never delay or stop rinsing for this.
Something stuck in the eye, a chemical in the eye, or any change in sight: call the medical officer at once and open Someone needs help again.
Remove a loose particle and check the eye surface for scratches, as in the onboard procedure.

steps.text: Chemical powder: brush it off first, then rinse.

In weightlessness, cool the burn with wet cloths. The method: to be set by clinical review.
Water runs off more as on Earth. The cooling method: to be set by clinical review.
Take off clothing and jewellery near the burn, unless it is stuck to the skin.
Do not use ice, creams or gels, and do not burst blisters.
When it is cooled, lay cling film or a clean dressing over the burn, if the kit lists one. Do not wrap it around.
Keep the person warm. Do not over cool them.
Watch for a burned face, mouth or throat, a hoarse voice, or smoke exposure, and tell the medical officer.
Take their body temperature with the kit thermometer as its instructions say, to avoid over cooling. Record the number and the time. Never delay or stop cooling the burn for this.

Put the cuff on the bare upper arm and follow the device instructions, arm supported and still. The level that needs action: to be set by clinical review. Never delay or stop cooling the burn for this.

Clip the oximeter on a finger, hand warm, relaxed and still, until it shows one steady number. A normal number does not cancel serious symptoms. Take a still photo of the burn in good light for the medical officer, kept with the log. Never delay or stop cooling the burn for this.

If the face, mouth or throat is burned, the voice turns hoarse, there was smoke, or the burn is large or deep, or from a chemical or electricity, call the medical officer and open Someone needs help again.
Burn dressings if the kit lists them, pain relief and fluids, as in the onboard procedure.

steps.text: Protect yourself first: keep out of the affected air, and put your mask on before you help anyone if the kit lists masks or portable breathing apparatus. Then move the person to clean air, with a mask on them too if the kit lists one.
Chemical on the skin or in the eyes: rinse with plenty of water.
Note what it was (smoke, ammonia, another chemical or not known), how long they were in it, and whether a mask was on.
On a single cabin vehicle there is no clean module to retreat to. Masks and suits are the protection.
Keep watching them: signs can appear up to 2 hours later. Watch for cough, chest tightness, trouble breathing, burning or watering eyes, headache, dizziness, sickness or confusion.

If they are already still in front of the cameras, read their breathing rate there. Never delay a step for it. If it fails, count their breaths and enter the number. Never delay or stop getting to clean air for this.

If the habitat has sensors, read them for the substance, oxygen and carbon dioxide. The limits come from the vehicle's flight rules. Never delay or stop getting to clean air for this.
If they are not breathing normally once you are both in clean air, go back to the first screen and start chest compressions.
If anyone has trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion or burning eyes, open Someone needs help again.
Breathing support, and oxygen if an oxygen supply is aboard, as in the onboard procedure.
Medicines, as in the onboard procedure.

steps.text: Follow the vehicle's depressurization response: warn, gather, then work the problem.

Gather in the safe haven. If the habitat has sensors, read cabin pressure and oxygen to work out the reserve time, and retreat to the safe haven before it runs out. If it has none, retreat to the safe haven now.
On a single cabin vehicle, put your suit on at once, if the kit lists suits.
Watch yourself and others for low oxygen signs: fast breathing, headache, lightheadedness, dizziness, tingling, sweating, clumsiness, poor judgement, tunnel vision, an odd good mood.
Anyone with low oxygen signs gets oxygen by mask or suit, if the kit lists oxygen masks or suits, as in the onboard procedure.
Afterwards, if anyone has joint pain, tingling, or itchy or blotchy skin, go back to the first screen of Someone needs help and choose Decompression sickness after a spacewalk.
Once safe, ask about headache, dizziness, tingling, blurred vision, joint pain, itchy or blotchy skin, ear or sinus pain, chest pain or trouble breathing.

Clip the oximeter on a finger, hand warm, relaxed and still, until it shows one steady number. A normal number does not cancel serious symptoms. The level that needs action: to be set by clinical review. Never delay or stop the depressurization response for this.

If they are already still in front of the cameras, read their breathing rate there. Never delay a step for it. If it fails, count their breaths and enter the number. Never delay or stop the depressurization response for this.
If the habitat has sensors, read cabin pressure and oxygen. The limits and the reserve time come from the vehicle's flight rules. Never delay or stop the depressurization response for this.
If someone stops responding and is not breathing normally, once you both have air, go back to the first screen and start chest compressions.
If anyone gets worse, or has chest pain or trouble breathing, open Someone needs help again.
Treatment of decompression sickness, as in the onboard procedure.

steps.text: Report any symptom at once, even a mild one. Serious signs in the brain, nerves, lungs or heart end the spacewalk.

Treat joint or muscle pain, tingling or numbness, itchy or blotchy skin, weakness, confusion, vision change, breathing trouble or chest pain after a spacewalk as DCS until the medical officer says otherwise.
Bring the person back to full cabin pressure, and give oxygen by mask if the kit lists one, as in the onboard procedure.
Note when the spacewalk ended and whether the full prebreathe was done, when the symptom began and where it is, and whether it is getting worse.
Keep watching for new or worse symptoms: tingling, weakness, confusion, trouble breathing, chest pain, marbled or blotchy skin.

If any new sign appears in the brain, nerves, lungs or heart, or any symptom gets worse, open Someone needs help again.
Return to full pressure, and give oxygen by mask if the kit lists an oxygen mask, as in the onboard procedure.
If the kit lists a suit and oxygen for it, suit pressure treatment, similar in principle to diving treatment tables, as in the onboard procedure.

steps.text: Stay in the shelter area, behind as much stowage and equipment mass as you can.
Use the shelter covered with lunar soil, if the base has one.
Keep your personal radiation tracker on, if you have one.
If the habitat has radiation sensors or you have a tracker, keep watching them. How long to stay is set by flight rules and the onboard radiation monitors.
If the habitat has radiation sensors, or you have a personal tracker, read them. The levels that call for shelter are set by flight rules. Never delay or stop reaching the shelter for this.
After the event, ask about nausea, vomiting, headache, tiredness or skin redness. If anyone vomits, record the time of the first vomiting. Never delay or stop reaching the shelter for this.
If someone feels unwell, take their temperature with the kit thermometer as its instructions say. Record the number and the time. Never delay or stop reaching the shelter for this.

Treat nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, as in the onboard procedure.

steps.text: Get the adrenaline auto-injector from the kit, if the kit lists one. It is given as in the onboard procedure.
Sit them up if breathing is hard, or lay them down with legs raised, where there is gravity, if they are faint or dizzy. Do not let them stand or walk.
Note any swollen lips, mouth, tongue or throat, a tight throat or trouble swallowing, fast breathing or wheezing, a rash, and what they ate, touched or took. Ask about any known allergy.
Keep watching their breathing, any swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat, and how faint or dizzy they feel.

Ask when they last ate, whether they did hard exercise or a long task without food, whether they took anything, and whether they feel shaky, sweaty, hungry or confused.
Stay with them and watch whether the shaking, sweating, hunger or confusion goes away.

steps.text: Help them rest in the position that hurts least.

Call everyone and the medical officer at once if the pain started suddenly and is severe, they vomit blood, their poo is black and sticky, they cannot pee or pass wind at all, or they struggle to breathe.

Record where it hurts and whether it has moved, when it started and whether suddenly, whether it comes in waves or spreads to the groin, any fever or shivering, being sick or any blood, and whether pee and poo are normal.
Give no pain medicine unless the medical officer gives it, as in the onboard procedure.

steps.text: Stay with them, ask directly, and listen.
Remove anything that could be used to hurt themselves or others.
Keep a second crewmate with you. Do not deal with a volatile person alone.
Ask them: are you thinking about suicide, do you have a plan, have you taken anything, what would help right now. Ask the helper whether anyone has been hurt.
Keep watching them and stay with them. Speak calmly and listen.
Only if they agree: check their pulse and blood pressure with the oximeter and the cuff. Do not insist. Never delay or stop staying with them and removing anything harmful for this.
If they talk about suicide or a plan, or anyone cannot keep themselves or others safe, stay with them and open Someone needs help again.
Calming, medicines, and restraint as a last resort, as in the onboard procedure.
